title: Can I Dispute a Hard Credit Inquiry? | CreditDoc
h1: Can You Dispute a Hard Credit Inquiry? Rules, Steps, and Impact Explained
meta_description: You can dispute a hard credit inquiry if it’s unauthorized or inaccurate. Learn when disputes succeed, how to file, and the impact on your credit score.
primary_question: Can I dispute a hard credit inquiry?
questions_answered: Can I dispute a hard credit inquiry?

sections.heading: Can You Dispute a Hard Credit Inquiry? (Short Answer)
sections.content:
Yes, you can dispute a hard credit inquiry if it was unauthorized or reported in error. Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA), only inquiries you did not permit—such as those resulting from identity theft or creditor mistakes—are eligible for removal.

- Legitimate inquiries (for example, when you applied for a loan or credit card) cannot be disputed solely to improve your credit score.
- Unauthorized or inaccurate inquiries can and should be disputed with the credit bureaus.

The impact of a hard inquiry on your credit score varies depending on your credit profile. Generally, a single hard inquiry may cause a small, temporary drop in your score. The effect typically fades over time.

sections.heading: What Counts as an Unauthorized Hard Inquiry?
sections.content:
- Fraud or identity theft: Someone applied for credit in your name without permission.
- Creditor error: A lender pulled your credit without your consent or for the wrong person.
- Business or promotional pulls: These should be soft inquiries; if reported as hard, they are disputable.

Not disputable:
- Any inquiry you authorized, even if you were denied or changed your mind.

According to the FTC, over 20% of credit reports contain errors, but only a small fraction involve unauthorized hard inquiries.

sections.heading: How to Dispute a Hard Inquiry: Step-by-Step
sections.content:
1. Get Your Credit Reports
- Request free reports from all three bureaus at [AnnualCreditReport.com](https://www.annualcreditreport.com/).

2. Identify the Inquiry
- Note the date, creditor name, and bureau reporting the inquiry.

3. Gather Documentation
- Proof of identity (ID, Social Security number)
- Any evidence of fraud (police report, FTC Identity Theft Report)

4. File a Dispute
- Online: Each bureau offers online dispute portals.
- By mail: Send a dispute letter with documentation.

| Bureau      | Online Dispute Link                                    | Mailing Address                  |
|-------------|--------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------|
| Experian    | [Experian Dispute](https://www.experian.com/disputes/) | P.O. Box 4500, Allen, TX 75013   |
| Equifax     | [Equifax Dispute](https://www.equifax.com/personal/credit-report-services/credit-dispute/) | P.O. Box 740256, Atlanta, GA 30374-0256 |
| TransUnion  | [TransUnion Dispute](https://www.transunion.com/credit-disputes/dispute-your-credit) | P.O. Box 2000, Chester, PA 19016 |

5. Wait for Investigation
- Bureaus have 30 days to investigate and respond (FCRA §611).

sections.heading: What Happens After You Dispute?
sections.content:
- The bureau contacts the creditor to verify the inquiry.
- If the creditor cannot prove you authorized the inquiry, it must be removed.
- If the inquiry is verified as legitimate, it remains on your report.

Resolution Timeline:
- Most disputes are resolved within 30 days.
- If removed, your score may improve slightly, especially if you have few other inquiries.

sections.heading: Risks and Limitations of Disputing Hard Inquiries
sections.content:
- Frivolous disputes (challenging legitimate inquiries) are typically denied and may delay real corrections.
- Filing false disputes can be considered fraud under federal law.
- Disputing does not remove inquiries you authorized, even if you regret them.
- Multiple disputes in a short period may trigger bureau scrutiny.

Best Practice: Only dispute inquiries you are certain are unauthorized or inaccurate.

sections.heading: How Hard Inquiries Affect Your Credit Score
sections.content:
A single hard inquiry typically lowers your FICO score by a few points. The effect is greater for those with fewer accounts or shorter credit history. Multiple inquiries in a short period (such as rate shopping for a mortgage or auto loan) are often grouped as one if done within a certain window, depending on the scoring model.

Hard inquiries remain on your report for 2 years but only affect scores for about 12 months.

sections.heading: When to Consider Professional Help
sections.content:
If you suspect identity theft, have multiple unauthorized inquiries, or struggle to resolve disputes, consider consulting a credit repair company or legal aid. These services can help navigate complex cases and may assist with broader credit issues. Always verify credentials and check for compliance with the Credit Repair Organizations Act (CROA).

For ongoing protection, use credit monitoring services to detect new inquiries quickly.

For more on professional options, see our guide to credit repair companies.

faq_schema.question: Can I dispute a hard inquiry if I applied for credit?
faq_schema.answer: No. If you authorized the inquiry by applying for credit, it is considered valid and cannot be disputed solely to improve your score.

faq_schema.question: How long do hard inquiries stay on my credit report?
faq_schema.answer: Hard inquiries remain on your credit report for up to 2 years, but their impact on your credit score typically fades after 12 months.

faq_schema.question: Will disputing a hard inquiry hurt my credit score?
faq_schema.answer: No. Filing a legitimate dispute does not harm your score, but only unauthorized or inaccurate inquiries can be removed.

faq_schema.question: How quickly will my score improve if a hard inquiry is removed?
faq_schema.answer: If the inquiry is removed, any score improvement is usually seen within one to two billing cycles, depending on the bureau’s update cycle.

faq_schema.question: What should I do if I see multiple unauthorized inquiries?
faq_schema.answer: File disputes with each credit bureau and consider placing a fraud alert or credit freeze to prevent further unauthorized activity.
